strengths: Amazon Reviews 2023 is a large and practically useful resource, with roughly 571 million reviews, 48 million items, 33 categories, rich metadata, and fine-grained timestamps. The temporal split and explicit concern with train/test contamination are particularly appropriate for recommendation and time-sensitive retrieval.

The paper evaluates the representations across three complementary settings: sequential recommendation, conventional product search on ESCI, and the newly proposed complex product search task. This makes the study broader than a single downstream benchmark.

The language-item contrastive objective combined with an auxiliary MLM loss is simple and well motivated, and the paper includes useful ablations on multi-domain versus in-domain pretraining and on data-curriculum order.

BLAIR shows especially large improvements over BM25, RoBERTa, and SimCSE on Amazon-C4, supporting the claim that specialized language-item alignment helps for long, complex contextual retrieval. It is also competitive on several sequential-recommendation and ESCI metrics.

The release of multiple base/large checkpoints, code, dataset statistics, and concrete training details improves reproducibility and should make the resource useful to future NLP, IR, and recommendation research.
weaknesses: There is a concrete evaluation inconsistency: the prose says the sequential domains are Beauty, Games, and Office Products, but Tables 3 and 4 report Beauty, Games, and Baby. This must be corrected and the actual evaluation clarified.

The methodological novelty is limited. The model is essentially RoBERTa optimized with in-batch contrastive loss over review–metadata pairs plus MLM, an approach closely related to existing recommendation encoders and sentence-embedding methods. The main contribution is therefore the resource and benchmark rather than a new modeling paradigm.

The baselines are not sufficiently strong for a 2024/2026 submission. Beyond BM25, RoBERTa, and SimCSE, the comparison should include contemporary general-purpose sentence embeddings such as E5, GTE, Sentence-T5, Instructor, or BGE, as well as stronger recommendation-specific pretrained encoders where applicable.

The validity of Amazon-C4 needs stronger support. Queries are ChatGPT reformulations of long, 5-star test reviews, but the paper provides no human evaluation, hallucination analysis, item-identifiability checks, query-diversity analysis, or measurement of how well these synthetic queries reflect real user behavior.

Statistical evidence is limited: there are no multiple seeds, standard errors, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The advantages are also not uniform; for example, SimCSE outperforms BLAIR on several sequential-recommendation metrics, and the multi-domain ablation has mixed results.

The candidate-pool construction for retrieval is underspecified. It is unclear exactly how many in-domain and cross-domain candidates are ranked, and evaluation on sampled candidate pools does not by itself establish full-corpus retrieval effectiveness despite the use of NDCG@100.

Maximum input length is only 64 tokens, even though Amazon-C4 queries and especially item metadata are much longer on average. Truncation may remove precisely the complex contextual and attribute information the task is intended to test; longer-input models or ablations are needed.

Several data details require clarification, including the discrepancy between 48.18 million interacted items and 35.39 million metadata records, deduplication, in-batch false negatives, licenses, privacy/PII handling, and whether actual images/videos are released or only metadata references. Calling the dataset “multi-modal” may overstate what is available if only text or media links are provided.

Taken together, these issues do not invalidate the substantial resource contribution, but they limit confidence in a clear main-conference recommendation because the model is incremental and the evidence for broad superiority is not yet fully airtight.

strengths: Amazon Reviews 2023 is a substantial and timely resource: roughly 571.5 million reviews, 48.2 million items, 33 categories, metadata through September 2023, and finer-grained timestamps than prior Amazon review datasets. Its scale and recency make it potentially useful for retrieval, recommendation, and language-item representation research.

The paper takes leakage seriously by using absolute timestamps to construct the same 8:1:1 split for pretraining and downstream tasks and by pretraining only on the training split. This is more rigorous than the random splits common in recommendation research.

BLAIR is conceptually simple and reusable: RoBERTa-base/large encoders are aligned on user-review and item-metadata pairs with an in-batch contrastive loss plus an auxiliary MLM objective. The resulting embeddings can be inserted into both sequential recommenders and zero-shot retrieval pipelines.

The evaluation covers three complementary settings: sequential recommendation, conventional ESCI product search, and the newly formulated complex product search task. The authors also provide base/large models and ablations on multi-domain pretraining and initialization strategy.

The retrieval results show clear advantages over RoBERTa, MLM-only training, and the selected SimCSE checkpoints, especially on the long-context Amazon-C4 task. In sequential recommendation, BLAIR obtains the best reported result on many metrics, particularly in Games, and multi-domain pretraining improves downstream generalization in the ablations.

Reproducibility is supported by concrete data-filtering rules, the 30.8 million training-instance subset, model sizes, loss definitions, temperature and lambda values, learning rate, GPU count, and training time. The promised release of data, code, and checkpoints further strengthens the contribution.

The paper is clearly written, and Figure 1 effectively conveys the data construction, pretraining objective, and downstream applications. The work is squarely relevant to NLP, information retrieval, and recommender systems.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is incremental. Contrastive alignment between user language and item metadata is already the standard two-tower/sentence-embedding recipe, and the main novelty lies in the scale of the dataset, the training corpus, and the new evaluation setting rather than a new modeling principle.

The attribution of gains to the proposed objective is incomplete. SimCSE is an off-the-shelf checkpoint rather than a generic contrastive encoder trained on the same Amazon pairs, and there is no contrastive-only BLAIR variant. The MLM-only checkpoint shows that contrastive learning matters, but it does not isolate the contribution of the auxiliary MLM loss.

Sequential-recommendation evidence is uneven. BLAIR-large does not consistently outperform BLAIR-base and loses to SimCSE-large on Beauty and several Baby metrics, which complicates the claimed scaling effect. The experiments cover only three domains, report no standard deviations or significance tests, and omit several recent text-aware sequential recommenders. There is also a domain inconsistency: the text says Office Products while Tables 3 and 4 report Baby.

The retrieval baseline set is too narrow for a strong state-of-the-art claim. In addition to BM25, RoBERTa, and SimCSE, the paper should compare with contemporary encoders such as E5, Instructor, Contriever, Sentence-T5, GTE, or BGE, and ideally with hybrid retrieval or reranking methods.

Amazon-C4 is only semi-synthetic and may not reflect real information needs. The queries are ChatGPT rephrasings of long, five-star reviews, so they may encode review-specific style or shortcuts rather than genuine complex product-search intent. The main paper lacks human validation, hallucination/quality analysis, the full prompt and generation parameters, and warm versus cold item analysis.

The retrieval candidate protocol is unclear and apparently inconsistent. The text says that 50 random in-domain items plus the ground-truth item form the candidate pool, but Table 6 lists over one million items and BM25 obtains NDCG@100 of zero on Amazon-C4, which would be impossible if only 51 items were ranked. The authors must clarify whether ranking uses the full corpus or a sampled pool and describe how BM25 indexes fields.

The 64-token pretraining truncation is in tension with the long-context task: Amazon-C4 queries and item metadata average 229.9 and 539.0 characters, respectively. The paper should state the downstream maximum length, report how many inputs are truncated, and analyze whether truncation disadvantages long complex contexts.

Important curation details are missing: the strategy for downsampling to 10% of pairs, domain and popularity balancing, metadata field ordering, duplicate or near-duplicate removal, handling of failed generations, and statistics on item overlap between pretraining and evaluation. Without these, memorization of warm items cannot be separated from generalization.

Some claims are overstated. Image and video links in metadata do not by themselves make the processed contribution multimodal, and sequential recommendation is not zero-shot because the recommender is task-trained. The paper should also discuss data licensing, privacy, and bias risks associated with a large user-review corpus.

Taken together, these limitations prevent an unqualified main-conference claim of broad superiority, although the dataset, checkpoints, and multi-task empirical study still constitute a solid and potentially useful Findings-level contribution.

strengths: Amazon Reviews 2023 is a large, timely, and useful resource: roughly 571 million reviews, 48 million items, 33 categories, interactions through September 2023, richer metadata, and fine-grained timestamps. The timestamp-based splitting also directly addresses temporal contamination.

The paper provides practical pretrained representations in BLAIR-base and BLAIR-large, combining review–metadata contrastive learning with an auxiliary backbone objective. Training details such as initialization, hardware, learning rate, temperature, truncation, and model sizes are reported.

The newly introduced complex product search task and Amazon-C4 dataset target an important limitation of conventional keyword-based product search: retrieving items from long, contextual, multi-constraint natural-language descriptions.

The empirical study spans sequential recommendation, conventional product search on ESCI, and complex product search, together with ablations on multi-domain pretraining and data curricula. The results clearly show that MLM-only representations are insufficient for retrieval and that BLAIR is especially strong on Amazon-C4.
The promised release of the dataset, code, and multiple checkpoints strengthens reproducibility and should make the work useful to researchers in NLP, information retrieval, and recommender systems.
weaknesses: The model architecture and training objective are relatively incremental: BLAIR is a RoBERTa-based dual encoder trained with a standard supervised contrastive loss plus MLM. The main contribution is therefore primarily a resource, benchmark, and empirical study rather than a new modeling technique.

The validity of Amazon-C4 needs stronger qualification. Its queries are semi-synthetic outputs from a single ChatGPT model, and the paper does not report systematic human evaluation, generation settings, failure rates, or checks for distinctive brand/product-term leakage. Human queries or queries from multiple generators would make the benchmark more convincing.

The retrieval candidate construction is ambiguous and potentially easy. The text mentions both a large multi-domain pool and sampling only 50 in-domain items, while reporting NDCG@100. It should be made clear whether ranking is over the full item catalog, a fixed large pool, or a small sampled set, and full-corpus or hard-negative results would be more persuasive.

There are concrete reporting inconsistencies: the sequential-recommendation text names Office Products, whereas Tables 3 and 4 evaluate Baby; the Table 4 caption also mentions only Recall@10 and NDCG@10 although @50 metrics are shown. These should be corrected.

The sequential-recommendation gains are not uniformly dominant: for example, BLAIR-large loses several Baby metrics to SimCSE-large. Without repeated runs or statistical significance tests, broad superiority claims should be tempered, especially where differences are small.

The baseline set for product search is somewhat narrow. Strong contemporary embedding models such as Contriever, E5, GTE, BGE, or Instructor, and potentially LLM-based rerankers, would better establish whether BLAIR’s gains arise from domain pretraining rather than from weaker comparisons.

The actual first-release pretraining uses a 10% downsample of 30.8 million pairs, one epoch, and a 64-token limit, rather than the full 570-million-review corpus. This is reasonable computationally, but the framing should distinguish it from full-corpus pretraining and clarify the effects of truncation and scale.

strengths: The paper introduces a timely and practically important benchmark for evaluating LLMs as frozen semantic encoders across sequential recommendation, collaborative filtering, and product search.

Amazon Reviews 2023 is a substantial resource: roughly 570M reviews, 48M items, recent interactions through September 2023, finer timestamps, and re-parsed structured metadata. It should be useful beyond this particular benchmark.

The benchmark covers multiple established datasets and strong downstream architectures, while controlling downstream parameter counts and using frozen encoders. The appendix provides useful preprocessing, splitting, prompt, and evaluation details.
The complex-query product-search subtask is valuable, and providing both a semi-synthetic dataset and a real-world Reddit-based dataset is a good design choice.

The paper is clearly written, and the reported insights—especially the possible mismatch with MTEB, task-dependent scaling, and adaptor sensitivity—are relevant to both NLP and recommender-system research.
The promised toolkit and detailed appendices strengthen reproducibility and make extension to new encoders easier.
weaknesses: The central MTEB-comparison claim is not strongly supported statistically. Figure 2 appears to contain only six models, and the reported Spearman correlation of -0.476 has p=0.233. This is underpowered and does not justify a broad conclusion that BLAIR and MTEB rankings are unrelated; confidence intervals, per-task correlations, all eligible models, and controls for model-family dependence are needed.

Ranking stability is not adequately assessed. The paper does not report multiple training seeds, standard deviations, bootstrap intervals, or pairwise significance tests, despite many close NDCG scores. Borda aggregation over heterogeneous tasks and datasets may therefore be sensitive to small fluctuations.

The combined ranking mixes tasks with different candidate-set protocols and difficulty levels, including 50-candidate sampled retrieval and the much larger Reddit-Movie candidate space. Sensitivity analyses should show whether conclusions hold under alternative aggregation and evaluation protocols.

The validity of Amazon-C4 as a proxy for real queries remains only partially established. ChatGPT-generated rewrites of reviews may retain stylistic, brand, or target-item artifacts, and a high model-score correlation with Reddit-Movie does not by itself establish query realism. Human evaluation or explicit leakage tests would strengthen this claim.

Scaling conclusions are drawn mainly from the Qwen3 family and from otherwise heterogeneous models with different training objectives. The evidence is suggestive but not sufficient for broad claims about how encoder size interacts with downstream complexity.

The metadata and adaptor analyses are small in scope, involving few models and datasets and often very small differences without significance testing. Details such as how PCA is fitted and whether API versions or generation hyperparameters are fixed should also be made explicit.
The authors acknowledge English-only coverage and limited model/category coverage; these limitations materially constrain the generality of the benchmark's conclusions.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant gap between general text-embedding benchmarks and the distinct requirements of recommendation, where representations are used by downstream recommendation models rather than only for direct similarity search.

Amazon Reviews 2023 is a substantial resource: approximately 571 million reviews, 48 million items, recent interactions, structured metadata, and finer-grained timestamps, with useful comparisons to earlier Amazon and large-scale recommendation datasets.

BLAIR covers three meaningful scenarios—sequential recommendation, collaborative filtering, and product search—and includes both short-query and the newly proposed complex-query product-search setting. The semi-synthetic Amazon-C4 and real Reddit-Movies datasets are particularly timely.

The experimental design is reasonably controlled: encoders are frozen, adapters align representation dimensions, downstream model sizes are kept consistent, and established architectures such as UniSRec and AlphaRec are used. Reporting per-dataset NDCG and Borda aggregation also makes the benchmark easy to interpret.

Reproducibility is supported by a promised toolkit, detailed split and preprocessing rules, the query-generation prompt, metric definitions, and extensive appendices. The paper is clearly written and relevant to NLP, IR, and RecSys.
weaknesses: The central MTEB–BLAIR finding is statistically fragile. The correlation is computed over only 11 models selected from high-performing MTEB systems, and the reported Spearman coefficient of −0.476 has p=0.233, so it is not significant. The result is best treated as an exploratory observation rather than evidence of a robust mismatch.

The claim that Amazon-C4 is a reliable proxy for real complex-query evaluation is validated on only one real dataset, Reddit-Movies, using only 11 systems. The domains, candidate-set sizes, and annotation protocols differ substantially, and a high rank correlation may partly reflect general model quality rather than proxy validity. A human evaluation of query naturalness and target-item leakage in Amazon-C4 would also strengthen the claim.

Some evaluation choices limit realism and comparability. Amazon-C4 and ESCI use 50 sampled candidates per query, whereas Reddit-Movies uses roughly 50,000 candidates; heterogeneous split strategies are used across datasets; and Reddit labels are derived from upvoted forum suggestions rather than explicit relevance judgments. Traditional ID-based or non-LLM textual baselines would also help contextualize the low absolute NDCG scores.

Scaling, metadata, and adapter conclusions are based on limited and partly confounded comparisons. Scaling is controlled only within the Qwen family, while other models differ in training objectives and architectures. The metadata and PCA-vs-MRL studies cover only a few models and datasets, and the observed scaling pattern is mixed across sequential recommendation and complex search.

Reproducibility should be tightened by pinning proprietary embedding versions, retrieval dates, the ChatGPT snapshot used for Amazon-C4, random seeds, adapter dimensions, optimization epochs, and other hyperparameters. Stable dataset/toolkit URLs, licenses, and long-term availability plans for the very large dataset should also be explicit.

Generalizability remains limited: the benchmark is English-only, uses 11 encoders because of compute constraints, and draws Amazon sequential/CF experiments from three categories. These limitations are acknowledged, but they constrain the strength of broad conclusions about LLMs as semantic encoders.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap: general-purpose embedding benchmarks such as MTEB do not adequately predict which LLMs work well as semantic encoders for recommendation.

Amazon Reviews 2023 is a substantial resource contribution, with over 570 million reviews, 48 million items, recent interactions, finer-grained timestamps, and richer structured metadata than prior Amazon Review releases.

BLAIR provides a unified and reasonably comprehensive evaluation across sequential recommendation, collaborative filtering, and product search, including both short-query and the newly proposed complex-query setting.

The methodology is largely sound: encoders are frozen, downstream parameter budgets are controlled, established architectures such as UniSRec and AlphaRec are used, and splits, preprocessing, metrics, prompts, and candidate construction are documented in detail.

The complex-query product-search task is valuable, and the combination of a semi-synthetic Amazon-C4 dataset with a real Reddit-Movies dataset is a thoughtful design that balances scalability with realism.

The empirical findings are useful for practitioners, especially the weak association with MTEB rankings, task-dependent scaling behavior, sensitivity to adapter design, and the limited benefit of naively adding descriptions.
Reproducibility is strengthened by a benchmarking toolkit, detailed appendices, per-dataset results, an explicit synthesis prompt, and evaluation code/data-processing descriptions.
The work is highly relevant to NLP, information retrieval, and recommender systems and is likely to support future model selection and benchmarking research.
weaknesses: Some central correlational claims are statistically underpowered. The MTEB–BLAIR correlation is based on only 11 models and is not significant (p = 0.233), so it should be presented as exploratory evidence of weak association rather than a definitive mismatch; confidence intervals or bootstrap analyses would strengthen the claim.

The evidence that Amazon-C4 is a reliable proxy for real complex-query search is still preliminary: the 0.94 correlation is computed over only 11 models, Reddit-Movies is a relatively small single-domain test set, and high rank correlation does not by itself establish query realism or cross-domain transfer.

Amazon-C4 queries are synthesized with ChatGPT from 5-star reviews. Although the prompt and filtering are described, the paper would benefit from human evaluation of query naturalness, ambiguity, target-item leakage, and similarity to genuine information needs.

Generalizability is limited by English-only data, 11 encoders, a small number of Amazon categories, and reliance on proprietary models whose training data and future versions cannot be fully controlled.

The benchmark primarily uses item titles despite collecting much richer metadata. The title-plus-description analysis is limited to a few models and datasets, leaving the central question of how LLMs use heterogeneous recommendation metadata only partially answered.

The paper does not report variance across random seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance for downstream performance differences; many pairwise differences in the detailed tables are small and may not be robust.

The Borda-based overall ranking may be sensitive to task weighting, metric choice, and the mixture of adapter-based and zero-shot protocols. A robustness analysis across aggregation methods would increase confidence in the global ranking.

The scaling conclusions are partly confounded by differences in model architecture, training objectives, and data across the 11 LLMs. The Qwen family provides useful matched comparisons, but broader causal claims about parameter scaling require more same-family model series.
Persistent dataset/toolkit identifiers, licensing information, contamination checks, and archived model versions should be clearly provided to ensure long-term reproducibility.
